TerraTools User Manual

Installing TerraTools, finding your way around, and preparing your data.
Getting started · Chapter 1

TerraTools is a desktop application from IRRI-SAH that brings twenty-one plant-breeding and genetics analyses into one window.
You open a tool from the sidebar, load your files, press Run, and read the results as plots and tables that you can download.
Everything runs on your own computer, and R and Python are already built in; only Gene Prioritization needs an internet connection, because it asks public gene databases.

| # | Tool | Group | What it does
 | 1 | Genofile Converter | Data Analysis | The start of the chain: turns the HapMap, VCF or raw allele files of a genotyping company into the 0 / 1 / 2 input files of Mendelian Segregation and Linkage Mapping.
 | 2 | Phenotypic Data Analysis | Data Analysis | Multi-environment trial statistics: ANOVA, mixed models, BLUEs, heritability, G×E stability.
 | 3 | Mendelian Segregation | Trait Mapping | Tests every marker for the expected segregation ratio (1:1 or 1:2:1) to find distorted markers.
 | 4 | Recombination Analysis | Trait Mapping | Finds the crossovers of RILs or backcross-derived lines, the donor content of every line and the recombination hot and cold regions, with intragenic crossovers.
 | 5 | Linkage Mapping | Trait Mapping | Builds genetic linkage maps (Kosambi cM) from coded marker data, with a file ready for QTL Mapping.
 | 6 | Genotype Viewer | Trait Mapping | Draws graphical genotypes of every chromosome for each sample (CSV or VCF), with bright or publication-ready palettes.
 | 7 | QTL Mapping | Trait Mapping | Locates QTL as regions with left / peak / right markers using six mapping methods; compares methods.
 | 8 | QTL-Seq | Trait Mapping | Bulk segregant analysis with the Δ(SNP-index) method from reads, BAM files or a VCF.
 | 9 | In silico BSA | Trait Mapping | Bulked segregant analysis from the genotypes and the trait of every line of a mapping population: the extreme lines form the pools, with the Gw statistic that also finds over-dominant loci.
 | 10 | Diversity Analysis | Trait Mapping | Haplotype diversity metrics, clustering, PCA and a neighbour-joining tree for varieties.
 | 11 | GWAS | Trait Mapping | Genome-wide association with eight models; built-in rice 3K panel or your own VCF.

| 12 | PYBSA G-statistics | Trait Mapping | Bulk segregant analysis from GATK variant tables using the G-statistic and Δ(allele frequency).
 | 13 | Genes Extraction | Trait Mapping | Turns the QTL of QTL Mapping into base-pair intervals and lists the genes inside them.
 | 14 | Gene Prioritization | Trait Mapping | Ranks candidate genes for a trait from Ensembl Plants, Gramene, Plant Reactome, PubMed and (rice) Oryzabase.
 | 15 | Clustering & Genomic Selection | Genomic Selection | PCA and K-means clustering with a cluster-stratified training / testing split.
 | 16 | Additive Dominance | Genomic Selection | Additive and dominance genomic relationship matrices from SNP dosages.
 | 17 | BreedSight GUI | Genomic Selection | Deep-neural-network + random-forest genomic prediction benchmarked against classical models.
 | 18 | Optimal Cross Selection | Genomic Selection | Plans the crosses with the highest usefulness while keeping diversity.
 | 19 | Heterosis | Genomic Selection | Deep-learning GEBV prediction and screening of hybrid combinations.
 | 20 | Favourable Allele Analysis | Genomic Selection | Matches your rice 4K haplopanel genotype file with 166 known trait genes and shows which favourable alleles each line carries (rice 4K only, for now).

A Windows 10 / 11 (64-bit) PC, or a Mac with Apple Silicon (M1 or later) running macOS 12 or newer.
At least 8 GB of memory; 16 GB is more comfortable for deep-learning tools (BreedSight, Heterosis) and for large VCF files.
Your data as CSV or Excel files in the layouts described in this manual.
About 3 GB of free disk space for the program, plus room for your results.
Tip. Every chapter lists the exact file layout the tool expects and points to a small example file in the sample_data folder that accompanies this manual. Run an example first to see how a tool behaves, then replace it with your own data.
Getting started · Chapter 2

Run the installer (TerraTools_Setup.exe) and follow the prompts; tick Create a desktop shortcut if you want one. It installs TerraTools (by default in Program Files) together with its own R and Python runtimes — nothing else needs to be installed.
Start TerraTools from the Start menu, the desktop shortcut or the Launch TerraTools option on the last installer page. The first start takes a little longer while the program prepares itself.
To remove it later use Settings → Apps → TerraTools → Uninstall.

Open TerraTools.dmg and drag TerraTools onto the Applications folder.
Open TerraTools from Applications. The very first launch unpacks the built-in R runtime, which takes about a minute; later launches are quick.
If macOS says the app cannot be verified, the build you have was not notarized by Apple. Open System Settings → Privacy & Security, scroll down to the message about TerraTools and click Open Anyway (on macOS 14 and older you can instead right-click the app and choose Open). You only need to do this once.
Note. A notarized build opens without any prompt. Which kind you have depends on how the release was published; the disk image contains a READ ME FIRST.txt only when approval is needed.

While a tool runs, it writes its working files to a temporary folder. Nothing is lost when you switch tools, but the temporary copies are not meant to be kept:
use the Download buttons (Excel, CSV, PNG, ZIP) to save results where you want them. Each button opens an ordinary Save As window.
Getting started · Chapter 3

Plots: every plot is an image on a white background, shown whole and never squeezed; the plots of a tab are arranged in two columns (one column in a narrow window); click it to open it full size in a pop-up (click outside it or press Esc to close). Every plot has its own Download PNG button, and pages with several plots offer Download all as PNG.
Tables: use the Filter rows… box to search, scroll sideways for more columns, and use the download button next to the table to get the complete data as CSV or Excel.
Status line: under the Run button. Errors are written there in plain words — read them first, they usually say exactly which file or setting to fix.
Getting started · Chapter 4

Most problems people meet come from the input files, not from the analyses. These rules apply to every tool.
File types. CSV (comma-separated, UTF-8) or Excel .xlsx, as stated for each tool. Save from Excel with File → Save As → CSV UTF-8.
One header row with column names, unless the tool says otherwise (QTL Mapping's genotype file has three header rows).
IDs must match across files, exactly. Line_01, line_01 and Line 01 are three different names. Avoid leading or trailing spaces. Chromosomes must be written the same way everywhere (3 in one file and Chr3 in another will not match).
No merged cells, no notes or totals rows, no blank rows inside the data. Put comments in a separate sheet or file.
Decimals use a dot (5.25, not 5,25). Do not use thousands separators in positions.
Keep names simple: letters, digits, underscore and hyphen. Very long names are fine but make tables hard to read.

| Tool | Genotype coding | Missing values
 | Genofile Converter (input) | alleles as sent by the company: HapMap AG, VCF 0/1, raw A:G; the output is coded 0 / 1 / 2 / −1 | NN, ./., -, N:N … (becomes -1)
 | Mendelian Segregation | 0 / 1 / 2 (RIL: 0 and 2) | Codes you list in the settings (default NA, ., -9); add -1 if you use it
 | Linkage Mapping | 0 = parent 1, 1 = heterozygous, 2 = parent 2 | -1 (or blank)
 | Genotype Viewer | A / H / B, or 0|0 / 0|1 / 1|1, or 0/0 / 0/1 / 1/1 (or a VCF) | N, .|. or ./.
 | QTL Mapping | 0 / 1 / 2 (RIL: 0 and 2) | any negative value (-1) or blank; filled automatically from neighbouring markers
 | GWAS | 0 / 1 / 2 dosage or −1 / 0 / 1 centred, as you choose (a file with only 0 and 1 must be told which); VCF: diploid genotype calls | NA or blank, -9, -99, -999; other codes can be listed
 | Clustering & Genomic Selection | 0 / 1 / 2 | -1
 | Additive Dominance | 0 / 1 / 2 | blank or NA (filled by mean, median or zero)
 | Diversity Analysis | haplotype block numbers (0 is a real code) | -1 or blank
 | BreedSight, Heterosis | numeric marker values (0 / 1 / 2) | none allowed — impute first
Watch out. Different tools treat the missing code differently. A -1 that is read as a real genotype (for example in Mendelian Segregation if you forget to list it) silently changes the result. Check the table above before loading a file.

The sample_data folder that comes with this manual holds one small, simulated example for every tool, in exactly the layout the tool expects.
The screenshots in this manual were made with these files. They are quick to run and a good template: open one in Excel, replace the values with your own, and keep the header and the column order.

One chapter per tool: the files it needs, what to click, what the settings mean and how to read the results.
Data Analysis · Chapter 5

The start of the chain. Genotyping companies deliver alleles — A/G, AG, 0/1 — in HapMap, VCF or spreadsheet files, but the analyses of TerraTools read genotypes coded against the two parents
(0, 1, 2). The Genofile Converter reads the company file, codes every individual against the parents you name, and writes one coded genotype table — the starting point for the other analyses.

One genotype file from the company, in one of three formats; the format is detected from the file.
 | Format | What it looks like | Calls
 | HapMap (.hmp.txt) | Tab-separated, one row per marker: rs#, alleles, chrom, pos, strand … QCcode, then one column per sample. | AA, AG, GG; a single letter is a homozygote (A) or an IUPAC code (R = A/G); NN is missing.
 | VCF (.vcf, .vcf.gz) | #CHROM POS ID REF ALT … FORMAT, then one column per sample. The GT field is read. | 0/0, 0/1, 1/1 (or with |); ./. is missing. More than two alleles are handled.
 | Raw allele calls (Excel, CSV) | One row per marker: Marker, Chromosome, the parents P1 and P2, then one column per individual. | A:G, A/G, A|G or AG; - or N is missing.
Raw allele sheet (Excel or CSV): Marker, Chromosome, the parents P1 and P2, then one column per individual.
 | Marker | Chromosome | P1 | P2 | F2_001 | F2_002 | F2_003 | F2_004 | …
 | SNP1_01 | 1 | A:A | G:G | A:G | G:G | G:G | A:G | …
 | SNP1_02 | 1 | C:C | T:T | C:T | T:T | T:T | C:T | …
 | SNP1_03 | 1 | A:A | C:C | A:A | C:C | C:C | A:C | …
 | SNP1_04 | 1 | G:G | T:T | G:G | T:T | T:T | G:T | …
 | SNP1_05 | 1 | A:A | G:G | A:A | G:G | G:G | A:G | …
Example files: sample_data/genofile/genofile_hapmap_example.hmp.txt, sample_data/genofile/genofile_raw_alleles_example.xlsx, sample_data/genofile/genofile_vcf_example.vcf
Key point. The parents define the codes. A marker is coded only when both parents are called, each is homozygous, and they carry different alleles. An individual is then 0 when it has Parent 1's allele twice, 2 for Parent 2's allele twice, 1 with one of each, and -1 when it is missing or carries an allele neither parent has.

Open Genofile Converter (Data Analysis) and click Browse. Choose the file; the page shows the format it found (change it with the three buttons if it is wrong) and a preview.
HapMap and VCF: in Parents and samples choose Parent 1 and Parent 2 from the samples of the file (names such as P1 and P2 are found automatically). Samples that are not part of the population — controls, other lines — can be listed under Samples to leave out. Raw sheet: check the columns found for Marker, Chromosome, P1 and P2 and the allele separator; every other column is an individual.
HapMap and VCF: set the Output settings — the marker names (as in the file, or chromosome_position, for example chr01_1044946, which carries the physical position of the marker, read by analyses such as Linkage Mapping), the chromosome labels (Chr01 becomes 1) and whether markers on scaffolds are left out.
Click Convert Genotype File. The Results tab opens.
Download the coded file (CSV, or Excel with the reports), or continue with it in another tool with the buttons under Your converted file: Mendelian Segregation, Linkage Mapping and Recombination Analysis open with the converted file already loaded.

Summary cards: markers in the file, markers coded (kept), left out, individuals and the share of calls that are missing or unexpected.
Your converted file: one table with a row per marker and the columns Marker, Chromosome and one column per individual, filled with 0 (Parent 1 allele), 1 (heterozygous), 2 (Parent 2 allele) or -1 (missing / unexpected). The parents are not in the table. It is offered as a CSV (the table) and as an Excel workbook (the same table on the first sheet, then Marker_Details — the missing and unexpected calls of each marker, Excluded_Markers — every marker left out and why, and Summary — the settings and counts).
Why markers were left out: a parent call missing, a parent heterozygous, both parents with the same allele, or (when chosen) an unplaced contig. Genotype codes shows how many calls were 0, 1, 2 and −1.
Coded markers and Markers left out list the first rows, with the reason for each marker that was left out.
Note. A very large file (a table of more than 1.5 million coded cells) is not written as an Excel sheet, which would take minutes to write and open; the table is then given as the CSV only, and a small workbook holds the reports. HapMap and VCF files are read line by line, so even a large file is converted without filling the memory.
Tip. Convert once, then use the files in every analysis of the same population. If you used chromosome_position marker names, Linkage Mapping can read the physical positions from them.
Data Analysis · Chapter 6

Analyses multi-environment field trials laid out as an augmented RCBD, an RCBD or an alpha-lattice: descriptive statistics, ANOVA, mixed models with BLUEs, variance components and heritability,
correlations, clustering, PCA and genotype-by-environment stability (including AMMI).

A CSV or Excel file with one row per plot. Columns are found by their name, in any order (capital letters and spaces around a name do not matter). There are two kinds of columns.
 | Column name | Needed for | What it holds
 | Genotype | all designs | Name of the variety or line. Checks and new entries both go here; a genotype that appears more than once in an environment is treated as replicated.
 | Environment | all designs | Location, season or year label. At least two different environments are needed.
 | Rep | all designs | Replicate number. Augmented RCBD: use 1 in every row if the trial is not replicated. RCBD and alpha-lattice: each genotype appears once in every Rep.
 | Block | augmented RCBD, alpha-lattice | Block number. Augmented RCBD: every block holds all the checks and some new entries. Alpha-lattice: the incomplete block, numbered inside its Rep (1, 2, 3 … again in every Rep). An RCBD does not need it.
 | Any other column, for example Yield, PlantHeight, DaysToFlower | — | A trait. Every other numeric column is a trait. Leave a cell empty (or write NA) when a trait was not measured. A 0 is also read as not measured (a note lists where this happened); switch this off with Treat 0 as missing if zeros are real values.
 | Plot, Row, Column, Range, Year, Season, Entry, Line.type, Remarks | — | Layout and label columns. They are not treated as traits.
Example: multi_environment_trial_example.csv
 | Genotype | Environment | Rep | Block | Row | Column | Plot | Year | Season | Yield | PlantHeight | DaysToFlower
 | Geno01 | Env_2023_Wet | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 101 | 2023 | Wet | 7.07 | 100.7 | 87.8
 | Geno02 | Env_2023_Wet | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 102 | 2023 | Wet | 5.24 | 100.8 | 84.6
 | Geno03 | Env_2023_Wet | 1 | 1 | 1 | 3 | 103 | 2023 | Wet | 6.78 | 107.7 | 86.3

| Geno04 | Env_2023_Wet | 1 | 1 | 1 | 4 | 104 | 2023 | Wet | 5.5 | 103.5 | 82.4
 | Geno05 | Env_2023_Wet | 1 | 1 | 1 | 5 | 105 | 2023 | Wet | 6.87 | 100.3 | 85.1
At least 3 genotypes and 2 environments are needed.
Trait columns must be numeric. The tool reads the file once and lists the traits it found (those with at least one value); every analysis tab then lets you tick the traits it should use.
The file can hold other columns in any position (a plot number, a field map, comments). If a column the design needs is missing, a warning under the file name names it.
Each genotype should appear in each environment (ideally repeated in reps); unbalanced data still run but give less precise estimates.
The first rows of each design look like this (the Plot, Yield and PlantHeight columns are examples; you can have as many trait columns as you like):

 | | New07 | Env1 | 1 | 1 | 102 | 6.1
 | | Check2 | Env1 | 1 | 1 | 103 | 5.3
 | | New21 | Env1 | 1 | 2 | 201 | 5.8
 | RCBD | Geno05 | Env1 | 1 | (none) | 101 | 6.8
 | | Geno03 | Env1 | 1 | (none) | 102 | 7.8
 | | Geno05 | Env1 | 2 | (none) | 201 | 6.5
 | Alpha-lattice | Geno05 | Env1 | 1 | 1 | 101 | 6.8
 | | Geno03 | Env1 | 1 | 1 | 102 | 7.8
 | | Geno12 | Env1 | 1 | 2 | 105 | 5.9
 | | Geno05 | Env1 | 2 | 3 | 201 | 6.5
Example files: sample_data/phenotypic/alpha_lattice_example.csv, sample_data/phenotypic/augmented_rcbd_example.csv, sample_data/phenotypic/multi_environment_trial_example.csv, sample_data/phenotypic/rcbd_example.csv

Choose the layout of your trial under Experimental Design. It decides which blocking terms the ANOVA, the mixed models (BLUEs) and the heritability use.
 | Design | Columns needed | How the file should look | Blocking terms
 | Augmented RCBD | Genotype, Environment, Rep, Block | Checks repeated in every block, new entries once. Use one Rep (all 1) if the trial has no replicates. | Block, fixed. Rep is used only if every Rep + Block group holds a check
 | RCBD | Genotype, Environment, Rep | Every genotype once in each replicate; the replicate is the block. The Block column is not used. | Rep
 | Alpha-lattice | Genotype, Environment, Rep, Block | Incomplete blocks inside each replicate. Number the blocks inside each Rep (1, 2, 3 … in every Rep); block 1 of Rep 1 and block 1 of Rep 2 are treated as different blocks. | Rep, and Block within Rep

The augmented RCBD follows the classical augmented-design analysis. The checks are the genotypes that occur more than once in the environment. A block is the value of the Block column; if the file has several Reps and every Rep + Block group holds a check, the blocks are the Rep + Block groups instead (a Rep column that only numbers the repeats of the checks is ignored, and the Design Check tab says so). Block effects are estimated from the checks alone, every genotype's adjusted mean (BLUE) is its value corrected for its block, and the error term has (checks − 1) × (blocks − 1) degrees of freedom. The ANOVA of each environment has two parts — treatments adjusted for blocks, and treatments ignoring blocks, each split into checks, new entries and checks versus new entries — and the Design Check tab adds the standard errors of the differences between two checks, two new entries in the same block, two new entries in different blocks, and a new entry and a check. If the checks are not repeated across the blocks (or every block holds the same genotypes) the genotypes cannot be separated from the blocks; the analysis then treats the blocks as random and says so in the Design Check tab.
With RCBD and alpha-lattice the replicates (and blocks) are treated as nested in their environment, so “Rep 1” of one environment is not the same as “Rep 1” of another. The pooled mixed model (BLUEs across environments) and the heritability use random blocks for all designs. The pooled ANOVA table of the RCBD and alpha-lattice is a true analysis-of-variance table (degrees of freedom, sums of squares, F and p); in the alpha-lattice the genotype line is adjusted for the incomplete blocks.

The Design Check tab lists, for each environment, the number of plots, genotypes, replicates and blocks, the block size and how often each genotype occurs. It also warns when the file does not look like the chosen design — for example genotypes missing from a replicate in an RCBD, a single block per replicate in an alpha-lattice, or no repeated checks in an augmented design.
The example files augmented_rcbd_example.csv, rcbd_example.csv and alpha_lattice_example.csv show the layout of each design; multi_environment_trial_example.csv is a three-replicate trial in which every genotype is in every replicate; analyse it as an RCBD (under the augmented design it falls back to random blocks and says so).
Note. Pick the design that matches how the trial was planted. The same file can be analysed with any of them, but a wrong choice gives wrong error terms: an RCBD model on an augmented trial ignores the block effects, and an alpha-lattice model needs Block numbers that really are incomplete blocks.

Open Phenotypic Data Analysis and load the file in Data & Design. A summary shows the design, plots, accessions, environments and traits, with a table of the traits and the design check.
Choose the experimental design, whether to analyse all environments or only some, whether 0 counts as missing, and the colour scheme.
Open Analyses, pick an analysis (Descriptives, Environments, BLUEs, ANOVA, Heritability, BLUPs, Correlation, PCA, Clustering or Stability & G×E), choose its traits and options and click its Run button. Every analysis runs on its own, so you can run only what you need; results stay until you change the data settings.
Use Downloads for the Excel workbook of everything run so far, the ANOVA workbook, the BLUPs workbook, all figures (300-dpi PNG and vector PDF) or everything in one zip.

| Analysis tab | What you get
 | Descriptives | Mean, SD, CV, range, quartiles and shape of every trait (all environments, then each), box and violin plots per environment and the distribution of one trait.
 | Environments | Accession means and ranks in every environment, how the ranks change, and the correlation between environments.
 | BLUEs | Adjusted means (BLUEs) of every accession within each environment and over all environments from a mixed model; the standard errors of differences are added to the Design Check.
 | ANOVA | One analysis-of-variance table per trait with every environment and the pooled analysis side by side (DF, SS, MS, F, P, CV), a plot of where the variation comes from, and residual and normal Q-Q plots of one trait.
 | Heritability | Genotypic, G×E, block and error variance components and heritability on a plot and on an entry-mean basis, per trait, environment and pooled.
 | BLUPs | The best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) of every accession per trait and environment (and across environments), with its standard error, reliability, predicted value and rank, plus the Cullis H² and mean reliability of each model. Download the table as a CSV or the BLUPs workbook. In an augmented design the checks are fixed effects and are not listed (see BLUEs).
 | Correlation, PCA, Clustering | Relationships between traits (Pearson, Spearman or Kendall with P values), a PCA biplot and variance explained, and clusters of accessions (K-means or Ward hierarchical) with their trait means.
 | Stability & G×E | Wricke ecovalence, Finlay-Wilkinson slope, AMMI scores and ASV of every accession, with the stability, G×E and AMMI1 biplots.

Every figure can be saved as a 300-dpi PNG or as a vector PDF, and every table as a CSV. A message box above the results lists notes, warnings and errors of that analysis (for example when an environment has too little data).
Note. BLUPs come from the same mixed model as the Heritability tab, so their genotypic variance is the same. The standard errors and reliabilities are computed from the full mixed-model equations (they include the uncertainty of the fixed effects). H² Cullis = 1 − (mean variance of a difference between two BLUPs) / (2 Vg) (Cullis, Smith and Coombes 2006); it equals the classical entry-mean H² in a balanced trial and is the better figure when replication is unequal. Mean reliability = 1 − mean(PEV) / Vg is a slightly different number.
Tip. Heritability is a property of the trial, not only of the trait: it grows with replication and with the number of environments. Compare it between trials with that in mind.
Trait Mapping · Chapter 7

Checks whether each marker segregates in the ratio Mendel predicts, and flags the markers that do not (segregation distortion).
Run it before building a linkage map or mapping QTL, so that badly behaved markers can be removed.

One CSV file: a marker per row, the first column the marker name, the second the chromosome, and one column for every individual in the population.
Genotypes as they come from a genotyping company (HapMap, VCF, A:G calls) are converted to this layout by the Genofile Converter (chapter 5), which has a Mendelian Segregation shortcut under Your converted file.
Example: mendelian_RIL_example.csv
 | Marker | Chromosome | RIL001 | RIL002 | RIL003 | RIL004 | RIL005 | …
 | M1_01 | 1 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 0 | …
 | M1_02 | 1 | 2 | 0 | 2 | 2 | 2 | …
 | M1_03 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 0 | 2 | …
 | M1_04 | 1 | 0 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | …
 | M1_05 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | …
Genotypes are 0, 1 and 2 (homozygous parent A, heterozygous, homozygous parent B). In a RIL population most calls are 0 or 2.
Every marker is tested against the model of the population you choose. Calls that the model does not contain (heterozygotes in a RIL, for example) are not used in the test and are counted in the summary. A marker with too few calls to ever reach α is reported as inconclusive, not as passed.
Missing values are whatever you list in Missing Data (see below).
The file that Linkage Mapping writes for QTL Mapping (markers across, one row per individual, with a Chromosome and a Position row) is accepted too; it is turned into one row per marker automatically.
Example files: sample_data/mendelian/mendelian_RIL_example.csv

Open Mendelian Segregation and click Browse to load the genotype CSV.
Choose the population type, the significance threshold (α) and the multiple-testing correction, and check the missing-data codes.
Click Run Segregation Test. The Results tab opens when it finishes.

| Population | Classes tested | Expected ratio | Test
 | RIL, DH | 0 and 2 | 1 : 1 | Exact binomial. Heterozygous calls (1) are not part of the test.
 | BC1 to parent 1 (BC1P1) | 0 and 1 | 1 : 1 | Exact binomial. Class 2 cannot occur.
 | BC1 to parent 2 (BC1P2) | 1 and 2 | 1 : 1 | Exact binomial. Class 0 cannot occur.
 | F2 | 0, 1, 2 | 1 : 2 : 1 | Exact multinomial.
 | F3 | 0, 1, 2 | 3 : 2 : 3 | Exact multinomial.
 | F4 | 0, 1, 2 | 7 : 2 : 7 | Exact multinomial.
An F1 is refused: all its plants are heterozygous, so there is no segregation to test. The two backcross directions are separate types because the expected classes differ, and a backcross is never tested as a RIL.
Both tests are exact, so they stay valid when a marker has few calls. The binomial test compares the two classes with 1 : 1. The multinomial test lists every possible outcome for the number of calls and adds up the probability of all outcomes that are no more likely than the one observed; with more than 200 calls the expected counts are large and the χ² approximation is used. A marker is inconclusive when it has no usable call, or so few that even the most extreme outcome could not give a p-value below α (for a two-class marker, fewer than 6 calls at α = 0.05). It is neither called distorted nor passed, and it does not take part in the multiple-testing correction.
 | Setting | What it does
 | Population type | Each type has its own model, and a type without one is refused (see the table above). Choosing the wrong type tests the wrong ratio, so set it to the generation you genotyped.
 | Significance threshold (α) | A marker is called distorted when its corrected p-value (p_adj) is below α.

| Multiple-testing correction | FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg), the default, Bonferroni, or None (raw p). Testing hundreds of markers at a raw α of 0.05 flags many by chance alone, so a correction is recommended. It is applied over the conclusive markers (inconclusive ones are left out), before unplaced markers are dropped.
 | Missing data | Comma-separated codes counted as missing. The default is NA,.,-9,-1.
 | Keep only markers with a known chromosome | Drops markers without a chromosome (unplaced markers) from the results.

The Results tab draws three plots, each with its own Download PNG button.
Segregation plot (−log10(p) by marker): a Manhattan plot: every point is a marker, placed by its index along the file and coloured by chromosome (the legend Chr is below the plot). The dashed line is the cut-off of the chosen correction as a raw p-value (Bonferroni: α divided by the number of markers; none: α; FDR: the largest p-value among the markers called distorted, and no line when none is). Markers above the line are distorted. A cluster of points above the line on one chromosome usually means a genuinely distorted region, not several bad markers.
Heterozygosity plot: the percentage of heterozygous calls of every marker, placed and coloured like the segregation plot. A dashed line marks the heterozygosity expected in the chosen population (50 % in an F2 or a backcross, 25 % in an F3, 12.5 % in an F4); RILs and DHs are homozygous, so a marker with many heterozygous calls (or a whole chromosome that sits higher) deserves a check for genotyping errors or residual heterozygosity.
Distortion summary: the percentage of distorted markers on each chromosome, which shows at a glance where the distortion is concentrated.
Summary: the population, markers tested, inconclusive markers, markers flagged distorted, markers passing the quality check, and the calls that the model does not contain.
Full Results (CSV): every marker with its counts (c0, c1, c2), n (calls used in the test), n_unexpected, the test used, χ², p, p_adj, call (distorted, not distorted, inconclusive or no data), heterozygosity, −log10 p and the genotype calls.
Filtered Markers (CSV): the markers called not distorted, i.e. that pass the quality check, with their genotypes. Inconclusive markers are not in it.

LM-ready File (XLSX): the same markers as just Marker, Chromosome and the genotype calls, ready to load in Linkage Mapping.
Key point. Example with a real RIL population (Demo_Input_Files/02_Mendelian_Segregation: 334 markers, 176 rice RILs, type RIL, α = 0.05). All 334 markers are conclusive, and the 2,069 heterozygous calls are not part of the test and are listed in the summary. The correction changes the result a great deal: FDR flags 37 markers as distorted (chromosome 1: 16, chromosome 6: 10, chromosome 3: 7, chromosome 8: 3, chromosome 7: 1) and 297 pass; Bonferroni flags 8 (chromosomes 1, 3 and 6) and 326 pass; None flags 95, mostly by chance. The heterozygosity plot stays at 3 to 9 %, as expected in RILs, and the distortion summary shows the distortion concentrated on chromosomes 1, 3 and 6.

section: A dense RIL map, and a population that is not a RIL
text:
Key point. A dense demo map (Demo_Input_Files/02_Mendelian_Segregation/input/coded_genotypes_RIL_4k_simulated.csv: 4,499 markers, 150 simulated RILs on 12 chromosomes, about 4 % missing and 1 % heterozygous). Type RIL, FDR: 156 markers are distorted and 4,343 pass. Most of the genome sits near zero in the segregation plot, and three regions rise above the cut-off, on chromosomes 3 (about 21 to 29 Mb), 9 and 6; the distortion summary shows the same three chromosomes. This is what a normal RIL gives: a few localised regions, not a scatter of markers. Bonferroni keeps only the strongest region (27 markers on chromosome 3), and None flags 571 markers on nine chromosomes.
Watch out. When almost every marker is distorted. If the segregation plot is far above the cut-off on every chromosome, the population is probably not the type you chose. An example is a backcross-derived set (a recurrent parent crossed in two or three times, then selfed) tested as a RIL: about 87 % of the calls were parent 1 on all twelve chromosomes, and 3,687 of 4,454 markers were flagged against 1 : 1. The test is working; the expected ratio is wrong. Choose the type that matches the generation, and use Distortion summary and the share of parent 1 to check the recurrent-parent content. A region that stands out against a flat background is distortion; a whole genome that is skewed is the population.
Tip. A distorted region is not always a problem: it can point to a gametic selection factor or a sterility locus. Compare with the map position before deleting a whole stretch of markers.

Recombination Analysis answers three questions about a mapping population of RILs or backcross-derived lines: where did the crossovers happen, how much of the donor genome does each line carry, and where along the chromosomes is recombination frequent or rare.
It replaces the set of R scripts that were run one after the other (crossover detection, rate along the genome, circos plot, intragenic crossovers) with one tool.

One table with a row per marker, giving the chromosome, the position in base pairs and the genotype of every line, coded 0 / 1 / 2 with −1 for missing. Two kinds of file are read:
A table with the recurrent parent in it (the layout of a VCF-style table): CHROM, POS, ID, optional REF, ALT …, then one column per sample (IRRI-370_GT, RIL-001_GT …). The parent's allele is called A, the other homozygous allele B (the donor).
A coded table from the Genofile Converter (Marker, Chromosome, then the individuals): there is no parent column, 0 is the allele of Parent 1 (A) and 2 the allele of Parent 2 (B). The position is read from the marker name (chr01_1044946). The Genofile Converter has a button that opens its result here.
Genotype table: CHROM, POS, ID, REF, ALT, then one _GT column per sample.

Open Recombination Analysis (Trait Mapping) and click Browse. The page reads the file and shows the number of markers, chromosomes and samples, the share of heterozygous and missing calls and a preview.
Under Parent and lines choose the recurrent parent (the page guesses it). Name the donor only if it is genotyped in the file. List samples that are not part of the population — the donor, controls, a line that failed — under Samples to leave out. Choose none for a coded table.
Set the smoothing (below), the bin size of the rate plot and whether the rice centromeres are shaded.
Click Run Analysis. The Results tab opens with the figures, the downloads and the tables.

section: Smoothing: the setting that matters most
text:
A genotyping error inside a block of the other parent's allele would look like two crossovers. TerraTools therefore overwrites every run of A or B calls shorter than a minimum block, given as a percentage of the markers of the chromosome (at least 3 markers). Three methods are offered:
 | Method | What it does
 | Original script | The first run shorter than the minimum takes the value of the run before it (the first run takes the value of the next one); repeated up to 50 times. Reproduces the results of the earlier R scripts exactly.
 | Shortest run first | The shortest run is merged into its longer neighbour, again and again, until every run has the minimum length. No limit on the number of passes.
 | None | Every isolated call counts as two crossovers. Useful only to see how much noise there is.
Watch out. The block size changes the numbers a great deal. In a simulation with 489 known crossovers in 80 lines, a block of 2 % recovered 405 of them, 3 % about 350 and 5 % only 264 to 290, depending on the method,, because real short donor segments are shorter than the block and are removed with the errors. On the lab's 4K data the same file gave 3,432 crossovers with the original script and 5,686 with the shortest-run-first method at 5 %. Choose the block from what you know about the shortest introgression you expect, report it with your results, and compare two settings before you rely on a count.

Summary cards: lines, informative markers (the parent homozygous and at least one line with the other allele; the others cannot show a crossover), crossovers, mean per line, mean donor % and, when the marker names carry genes, the share of intragenic crossovers.
Figures: crossovers per line and per chromosome; the genome-wide crossover rate (crossovers per line in each bin, with the centromeres shaded); donor content per line and per chromosome; the haplotype mosaic (one row per line, sorted by donor %; yellow = parent, red = donor, blue = heterozygous, grey = missing); a circos version of it; and, with genes, intragenic versus intergenic crossovers and the genes with the most intragenic crossovers.
Please note: lines with more than half of their calls missing (they cannot be used), very heterozygous lines, and a reminder that a crossover is only located to the interval between its two flanking markers.
Tables and downloads: the Excel workbook has the sheets Summary, Settings, Per_chromosome, Per_RIL, Crossovers, CO_rate_by_bin and Genes; the ZIP has the same tables as CSV files and every figure as a PNG. The crossover table gives, for each crossover, the line, chromosome, the two flanking markers and their positions (BP_start, BP_end), the middle of the interval, its size, the number of markers inside it, the direction (A→B or B→A) and, with genes, the type and the gene.
Note. Donor % per line is the average of the chromosomes, each the share of B among its A and B calls; the column Donor_pct_all_markers pools all markers instead. A line with no locatable crossover is counted in the mean per line with 0.

Tip. In backcross-derived lines (mean donor around 20 %) crossovers can only be seen inside donor segments, so the crossovers per chromosome say as much about where the donor was kept as about the recombination rate. Compare chromosomes with that in mind.

Builds a genetic linkage map the way JoinMap and Lep-MAP3 do: it checks which markers belong together (LOD), finds the marker order that the genotypes support, and estimates all distances together (multipoint maximum likelihood) in centiMorgans.
It writes a file that QTL Mapping can read directly. Genotypes from a genotyping company are converted to the 0 / 1 / 2 codes first, by the Genofile Converter (chapter 5).

An Excel file (.xlsx) with one row per marker: Marker, Chromosome, then one column per individual, coded 0 (homozygous for parent 1),
1 (heterozygous), 2 (homozygous for parent 2) or -1 (missing).
Example: linkage_F2_coded_example.xlsx
 | Marker | Chromosome | F2_001 | F2_002 | F2_003 | F2_004 | F2_005 | …
 | SNP1_01 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 0 | …
 | SNP1_02 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 0 | …
 | SNP1_03 | 1 | 0 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 0 | …
 | SNP1_04 | 1 | 0 | 2 | 2 | 1 | -1 | …
 | SNP1_05 | 1 | 0 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 0 | …
Key point. How the order is decided. Markers with identical genotypes share one position. The order is searched from the genotypes (smallest recombination between neighbours, then improved with the multipoint likelihood). If the marker names carry physical positions (chr02_16919033) that order is kept unless the genotypes favour another order by more than 3 LOD; markers without a position in their name are placed where they fit best. Markers on chromosome 0 (unplaced) are left out.
Note. Genotypes as they come from a genotyping company (HapMap, VCF, or A:G calls) are not read by this tool. Convert them with the Genofile Converter (chapter 5) first: its Linkage Mapping shortcut under Your converted file loads the converted workbook straight into the Upload tab. If the marker names carry the physical position (chr02_16919033), choose Marker names: chromosome_position there.
Example files: sample_data/linkage/linkage_F2_coded_example.xlsx

On the Upload tab, browse to the coded Excel or CSV file (the file written for QTL Mapping can be used again here) and choose the population type (F2 or RIL). A preview and the number of markers per chromosome appear.
On the Parameters tab set the filters (see the table) and click Run Analysis.
 | Parameter | What it does | Typical value
 | Missing data threshold | Markers with a larger share of missing calls are removed. | 0.30
 | Max recombination fraction (r) | Neighbouring markers with r at or above this value are not considered linked and get a 50 cM gap (the QC report warns when this happens). | 0.45
 | Marker order | The starting / reference order: automatic (re-sorts a chromosome by the physical position in the marker names only if the file lists it alphabetically), by physical position, or as in the file. | automatic
 | Map method | Find the best marker order (recommended) or keep my marker order. Both estimate Kosambi distances with all markers of a chromosome together and allow for 1 % genotyping error, so a single wrong call does not inflate the map. Markers linked more strongly to another chromosome, not linked to their own, or that add more than 10 cM to the map are removed and listed in the Removal Log. | find best order

QC Report: how many markers were removed and why (missing data, monomorphic, chromosome 0, map construction); the full list can be downloaded.
Results: the linkage-map table (marker, chromosome, position in cM), retained markers, all markers with their status, a chromosome summary (length, spacing, largest gap, log-likelihood, which order was used) and the recombination rate: when the marker names carry their physical position (chr02_16919033), the length of each linkage group in cM is set against its physical span, which gives kb per cM (the genome-wide value is shown at the top). A group whose cM order disagrees with the genome is flagged as partly out of order, and its rate is not reliable. The rate is also in the Physical Summary sheet of the Excel results.
File for QTL Mapping: the linkage map joined to your genotypes by marker ID and transposed — one row per individual, with marker, chromosome and position as the first three rows. Load it directly as the genotype file in QTL Mapping.
Map Plot, Density & RF, Cytogenetic: the map figure, marker density per bin, the recombination heat map of adjacent markers, and an interactive ideogram that shows the allele composition along each chromosome.
Tip. Choose chromosomes, theme and sizes in Plot Options and click Update Plot — changes apply to the finished analysis without re-running it.

The page is called Graphical Genotype Visualisation and is used for parent recovery: every chromosome of a line is drawn as a bar, coloured along its length by the genotype of the markers,
so that you can see which parent each stretch of chromosome came from and how much of the recurrent parent a line has recovered. It is built on GenoSee (Hashimoto 2024), with a choice of colour palettes,
parent names in the legend, rounded and shaded chromosomes, and PNG or vector-PDF images that are ready for a paper.

One genotype file, as CSV (or tab- / semicolon-separated text) or as a VCF (.vcf or .vcf.gz), with one row per marker:

Chromosome names are matched to the species you choose (1, chr1 and chr01 all mean the same chromosome). Markers on chromosomes that the species does not have are not drawn, and the Results tab says how many were left out.
Genotype calls can be written in one of three ways (use one way in the whole file):

For another species or genome version, use Add a species: choose its genome FASTA file (.fa, .fasta, also .gz) and type a name; the chromosome lengths are read from the file and kept for the next time.

Open Genotype Viewer (Trait Mapping, after Linkage Mapping) and click Browse to choose the genotype file. The number of samples and their first names appear under the box.
Choose the species. To draw only some samples, type their names in Samples to draw, separated by commas.
Choose the drawing mode, the colouring, the colour palette and the image quality (see the table below).
Optional: type what REF and ALT stand for in Legend names, for example Parent 1 and Parent 2.
Click Draw Graphical Genotypes. The Results tab opens with the images.
 | Setting | What it does

| Palette | Colours (REF / HET / ALT) | Use

The bars: each bar is a chromosome, drawn to scale in Mb. Each stretch is coloured by the genotype of the marker: with the default coding yellow is REF, blue is ALT, green is heterozygous and grey is missing. The colour changes where the genotype changes between two markers.
The legend (at the right in Normal and Compare mode, below the samples in Zoomed mode) names the colours. Type your own names in Legend names to show the parents.
Download: every image has a Download PNG button, Download all as PNG saves them together, and with Also save a vector PDF each image also has a PDF.

Adding the parents as sample columns is a good check: their bars are one colour all along.
Tip. For a figure in a paper: leave the marker names off, choose 600 dpi and tick Also save a vector PDF; use the PDF for the final layout.

Finds quantitative trait loci. Each QTL is reported as a region: a left flanking marker, a peak marker and a right flanking marker, with the
LOD, p-value and effect at the peak — following the usual interval-mapping practice (Lander & Botstein, Haley & Knott, Zeng, Churchill & Doerge, Broman & Sen).

1. Genotype CSV — three header rows, then one row per individual. Row 1 holds the marker names, row 2 the chromosome of each marker and row 3 its position in cM.
(The linkage-mapping tool writes exactly this file for you.)
Genotype file (first column and first markers shown). Rows 1–3 are marker, chromosome and position; each following row is one individual.
 | Marker | c1m01 | c1m02 | c1m03 | c1m04 | c1m05 | c1m06 | …
 | Chromosome | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | …
 | Position | 0 | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 | …

 | L002 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | …
 | L003 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | …
 | L004 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | …
2. Phenotype CSV — one row per individual: the first column is the ID (the same IDs as in the genotype file), then one column per trait.
Example: qtl_phenotypes_example.csv

Example files: sample_data/qtl/qtl_genotypes_example.csv, sample_data/qtl/qtl_phenotypes_example.csv

Open QTL Mapping. Load the genotype CSV, then the phenotype CSV. The Trait list fills with the phenotype columns — choose one.
Pick the mapping method and the threshold (see below). Leave the other settings at their defaults for a first run.
Click Run QTL Analysis. The Results tab shows the Manhattan plot and the QTL table.
 | Setting | What it does
 | Mapping method | SIM — one marker at a time. CIM — adds a few background markers (cofactors) to remove the effect of other QTL; the usual first choice. MQM — a larger background model. RF, SVR, XGBoost — machine-learning importance scores on a LOD-like scale (not true LODs).
 | Significance threshold | Fixed LOD (default 2.5), or a genome-wide permutation test (SIM / CIM / MQM): the phenotype is shuffled many times and the 95th percentile of the genome-wide maximum LOD becomes the threshold. For CIM and MQM every permutation repeats the whole method (the background cofactors are selected again and the composite scan is run again; Doerge & Churchill 1996), so it takes longer than for SIM (about 0.15 s per permutation for 250 lines and 4,000 markers). Permutation is the safer choice for publications.
 | Peak p-value cut-off | A peak must also have a nominal p-value below this (default 0.05).
 | Peak separation (LOD drop) | Two peaks on one chromosome count as separate QTL only if the LOD curve dips by at least this much between them (default 2).
 | Support interval — LOD drop | The QTL region extends left and right of the peak until the LOD has fallen by this amount; 1.5 gives roughly a 95 % interval (default 1.5). The first marker outside on each side is the flanking marker.
 | CIM cofactors / window | Maximum number of background markers and the distance (cM) around the tested position in which cofactors are ignored.
| Hold-out fraction | Fraction of individuals set aside before mapping. Leave at 0 to use everyone.

The Results tab has three parts. The buttons at the top download the Manhattan PNG, the Ideogram PNG, the QTL Table CSV and the Full Scan CSV (the LOD and the p-value of every marker).
Chromosome-wise Manhattan plot. Each panel is one chromosome: the curve is the LOD along the chromosome, the dashed line the threshold, the red diamond the QTL peak, and the shaded band the QTL region.
Chromosome ideogram. Every chromosome is drawn as a banded bar with its markers; each QTL is a bar between its flanking markers with a dot at the peak and the LOD written beside it, and the dot grows with the LOD. The ideogram is drawn with R, and it is the same drawing that the Compare Models tab uses for several methods at once.
QTL regions. The line above the table gives the number of QTL, the LOD threshold and how it was obtained (for the permutation test with CIM or MQM it also says that the cofactors were selected again in every permutation), the support interval, the number of missing genotypes that were filled in and the cofactors that CIM or MQM chose.

The Plot Settings tab sets the look of the two figures. The settings apply the next time you run an analysis or a comparison, so change them before you click Run QTL Analysis, and click Save Plot Settings when you are done.
Manhattan plot: height and width in pixels, the size and the colour of the points that do and do not reach the threshold, and the width and style of the threshold line (solid, dashed, dotted or dash-dot).
Ideogram: height and width in pixels, the dark band, light band and border colours of the chromosomes, and the smallest and the largest size of the QTL dots.
 | Column | Meaning
 | QTL_ID | Name of the QTL (chromosome and order along it).
 | Left_Marker, Peak_Marker, Right_Marker | The flanking markers and the marker with the highest LOD. The QTL lies between the flanking markers.
 | Interval_Size_cM, CI_Start/End | Width of the region in cM, and the interpolated positions where the LOD curve crosses the support-interval level.
 | LOD, P_Value, Genomewide_P | Strength of the evidence at the peak. Genomewide_P appears when the permutation threshold is used.
 | PVE_Marker_Percent | Percent of the trait variance explained by the peak marker.
 | Additive_Effect, SE_Additive | Half the difference between the two homozygous classes, in trait units. Positive means the higher-coded allele (genotype 2) raises the trait. For CIM / MQM it is estimated with the background markers in the model.
 | Dominance_Effect, Dominance_Class | Departure of the heterozygote from the mid-point (F2 only) and a label: additive, partial dominance, dominance, overdominance.

The Compare Models tab runs several methods on the same data, with the trait, threshold and settings of the Analysis tab (SIM, CIM and MQM are ticked at first; tick others to add them), and lines their QTL regions up; two methods found “the same QTL” when their regions overlap. It gives three things:
Multi-model ideogram: the chromosome map of the single run, with one lane and one colour per method: SIM pink, CIM bright red, MQM orange, RF grey, SVR light blue and XGBoost purple. Regions that several lanes share are the QTL that the methods agree on.
QTL counts per model: a bar chart of the number of regions each method found.
Comparison table (download as CSV): one row per region with its flanking and peak markers, its size in cM, the number of methods that detected it and which ones, the spread of the peak positions, and the mean and the maximum LOD and PVE. When the marker names carry their physical position (chr02_16919033) the region is also given in Mb, and Order_Check says whether the map follows the physical order, runs against it or differs from it between the three markers.
The Common QTL tab then keeps the regions that at least n methods agree on (set Minimum Models Detecting QTL, 2 to 6, and click Find Common QTL). It shows the same kind of ideogram for those regions, a bar chart of how many methods found each, and a table that can be downloaded as CSV.
Tip. The quickest way to a convincing result: run CIM with the permutation threshold, then compare CIM, SIM and MQM. QTL found by all three are the ones to trust.
Trait Mapping · Chapter 12

Bulk segregant analysis from sequencing data. Two bulks of plants, one with a high and one with a low trait value, are sequenced. For every SNP the SNP-index of a bulk is the share of its reads that carry the index allele; the Δ SNP-index is the high bulk minus the low bulk, so it lies between −1 and 1. A QTL shows as a stretch of the genome where the sliding mean of Δ rises above (or falls below) what chance alone would give.

BAM files (coordinate-sorted, with an index) of the high and the low bulk, and the reference genome (FASTA) they were aligned to. Parents are optional: with two parents TerraTools keeps only the SNPs at which they are confidently homozygous for different alleles; with one parent that parent must be homozygous; with none, the two bulks are compared on their own and the page warns that sites which are not polymorphic between the parents can remain.
Or VCF files of the high bulk and the low bulk (a parental VCF is optional) with an AD (allele depth) field. The genotype (GT) of a pooled bulk is never used as if it were a diploid genotype: only the read counts count. A single VCF that holds both bulks can be entered twice, with the two sample columns named under Advanced settings.
Optionally a gene annotation (GFF3 or GTF) to list the genes that overlap each QTL.
Also give the population type (F2, RIL or backcross) and the number of plants in each bulk: they set the spread of the Δ SNP-index expected by chance, which the confidence limits are built from.
VCF example: the sample columns hold GT:AD values. The AD part (reference reads, alternate reads) is what counts. In this file the HighBulk and LowBulk columns are used.

Trait Mapping · Chapter 13

In silico BSA is bulked segregant analysis without any pooled sequencing. You already have the genotype of every line of a mapping population and its trait value, so TerraTools sorts the lines by the trait, takes the lowest and the highest fraction as the low and the high pool, and compares the genotypes of the two pools at every marker.
It uses the Gw statistic of dQTG-seq (Li et al. 2022), which counts alleles and genotypes. Because it also looks at the heterozygotes, it finds over-dominant loci that allele-frequency methods (G′, ED, Δ SNP-index) cannot see.
Note. This tool is for a population in which every line is genotyped and phenotyped (F2, F3, IMF2, BC1, RIL, DH). If you have sequenced pools (a high bulk and a low bulk), use QTL-Seq or PYBSA G-statistics instead.

Counts. At every marker the two pools give a pool × allele table (2 × 2) and a pool × genotype table (2 × 3). A marker that cannot be scored gets no statistic (never a zero) and does not enter any window.
Statistics. G1 is the G statistic of the allele table, G2 that of the genotype table, and Gw = G1/(G1+G2) · G1 + G2/(G1+G2) · G2. A fully over-dominant locus has the same allele frequency in both pools (G1 near 0) but many more heterozygotes in one pool (a large G2), so only Gw sees it. The allele-frequency difference (the Δ SNP-index of QTL-seq) is reported too.
Windows. The genome is cut into non-overlapping windows of 250 kb, 500 kb and 1 Mb. The value of a window is the mean of the marker statistic over the scored markers it holds.
Threshold. Gw has no known distribution, so two pools of the same size are drawn at random from all lines many times and the largest window value of the genome is kept. The threshold of each window size is the (1 − α) quantile of those maxima, and the adjusted p-value of a window is (1 + the number of permutations that reach it) / (permutations + 1). This controls the error across all windows of that size.

Please note: warnings about the data, for example a heterozygosity that does not fit the chosen population or lines that were left out.
Loci across the window sizes: regions of the three sizes that overlap form one locus. Windows_that_found_it says how many sizes reach the threshold there (a locus found by all three does not depend on the window you chose), and Peak_spread_kb is how far apart the peak markers of the sizes lie.
Significant regions of every window size: one row per region and window size, with the left, peak and right marker and their positions, the adjusted p-value at the peak, the LOD (Gw / ln 10) and the Δ SNP-index (the allele of parent 2: positive means it is more frequent in the high pool). The Excel report adds the genotype classes at the peak. The Pattern column reads them: an allele-frequency shift (additive or dominant), or heterozygotes enriched in one pool without an allele shift (over-dominant). Also_significant_by_G1 and …_by_dAF say whether the allele-based statistics find the same region.
Closest to significant: shown for any window size without a significant region: the regions nearest to the threshold, with the fraction of the threshold they reach. They are not significant; treat them as leads.
Candidate genes (a separate step): choose a window size, the GFF3 or GTF annotation of the same genome assembly as your marker positions and a flank (100 kb by default). The tool lists the genes that overlap each region, nearest to the peak marker first, and saves them as Excel and CSV. They are positional candidates, not the causal gene.

Figures: Gw along the genome for the three window sizes; the loci found by each size; Gw compared with G1 and the allele-frequency difference; the genotype classes of the two pools at each peak; the trait distribution with the two pools; and the permutation null distributions.
Downloads: the Excel workbook (Summary, Settings, Window comparison, Loci, Regions, Thresholds, Windows, Closest to significant, Pools, Markers), a ZIP with the same tables as CSV files and all figures, and the main tables as single CSV files.
Key point. The example: the simulated F2 population of 300 plants has three QTL of about 8 % of the variance each. With 20 % pools, the F2 type and 1,000 permutations, all three window sizes find all three loci. The additive and the dominant QTL (chromosomes 3 and 1) are also found by G1. The over-dominant QTL on chromosome 2 (peak near 11.1 Mb) is found only through the genotype counts: 71 % of the high pool is heterozygous against 22 % of the low pool, with almost the same allele frequency in both.
Watch out. The permutation test treats the lines as exchangeable, which fits an F2, IMF2, backcross or RIL population from one cross. In a diversity panel with family structure, related lines in the same pool give false signals everywhere; use GWAS with a kinship matrix there. A very polygenic trait gives many regions: compare them with QTL Mapping before you choose candidates.

TerraTools expects genotypes that are already filtered (pruned for linkage, minor-allele frequency applied). It adds no further filtering: only markers without any variation, or without a valid chromosome and position, are dropped, and each missing call is filled with the mean dosage of its marker (not haplotype imputation: it ignores linkage disequilibrium and shrinks the variance of markers with many missing calls). Your genotype matrix itself is never edited. If fewer than 2 SNPs remain, the analysis stops with a message. The QC stage table is in the CSV and Excel report. The relationship matrix is VanRaden: K = ZZ′ / (2 Σ p(1−p)) with Z the genotypes centred by twice the allele frequency, computed from the observed calls before imputation. Under Advanced it can use LD-pruned markers or leave-one-chromosome-out matrices. If K is not positive semi-definite, negative eigenvalues are set to 0 and nothing else is changed. Principal components are taken from K and only used when you give a model a number of PCs (0 by default).

| Model | What it is
 | OLS | Marker-by-marker linear regression, optionally with PC covariates. With 0 PCs it is labelled uncorrected; with PCs, structure-corrected. It does not model relatedness.
 | MLM | y = Xβ + Zu + e, u ~ N(0, σ²ₐK), fitted by REML. The variance ratio is estimated once on the null model and the variance components are re-estimated for each marker; t test. The REML value is checked against a dense computation; the report says whether the check passed and whether the variance ratio reached the edge of its search range.
 | EMMAX | The same null model, with the variance ratio and the variance components fixed for all markers; a faster approximation.
 | GEMMA-style | The variance ratio is re-estimated for every marker (REML with a Wald test, or maximum likelihood with a likelihood-ratio test). It follows the same model as GEMMA but is not GEMMA: agreement with GEMMA is claimed only if you run the comparison (Advanced tab, needs the GEMMA program) and the numbers are within the stated tolerances.
 | FarmCPU, BLINK | Iterative multi-locus models, run by R packages that come with TerraTools: FarmCPU by rMVP and BLINK by GAPIT. TerraTools writes your genotypes, map and phenotype, calls the package with its own default settings (FarmCPU has one setting here, the number of iterations), and reads back each marker's p-value and effect. They use no kinship matrix, need physical marker positions (marker names such as Chr3_123456), and the packages give no standard error for BLINK. The percent variance explained is computed by TerraTools (marginal), because the packages do not return the markers they selected.

| mrMLM, FASTmrMLM | Run by the mrMLM R package, which is installed in the R that comes with TerraTools: TerraTools writes your genotypes (as −1 / 0 / 1), phenotype and the structure PCs in the package's file formats, calls the package, and reads its tables back. Which markers are QTNs, their effects and their LOD are the package's own results, and nothing is recomputed. The settings are the package's search radius (kb), the critical LOD (default 3) and the number of structure PCs. The package gives a first-step p-value for every marker and no standard error; the QTN list is judged by LOD, so no p-value is derived from it. The percent variance explained shown is computed by TerraTools from the joint model of the QTNs.

There is nothing to set. Every run reports Bonferroni (α = 0.05 over the markers tested) and Benjamini–Hochberg separately, and, for OLS, MLM, EMMAX and GEMMA-style, a threshold simulated under the model's own null fit (1000 replicates; the report gives its interval). Genome-wide significant follows Bonferroni. A marker with p ≤ 1/m that is not genome-wide is Suggestive. The 15 top-ranked markers of each model that pass nothing are listed separately as Exploratory and are never called significant. If no marker passes, the result says No genome-wide significant associations detected. Multi-locus models keep their own QTN criterion.

| Output | Meaning

 | Associations | One row per marker in three categories (genome-wide / QTN, suggestive, exploratory): model, SNP, chromosome, position, alleles, MAF, effect, SE, raw p, Bonferroni p, BH p, LOD, PVE and the criterion that applied. A multi-locus QTN keeps the LOD of its own model; no p-value is derived from that LOD.
 | Diagnostics | Per model: SNPs tested, invalid statistics, λ, smallest p, the p-value histogram, convergence and the REML check. λ is reported only. TerraTools does not call it good or bad and never rescales p-values with it (no genomic control).

| Model | Definition (fraction of the phenotypic variance)

Where an estimate cannot be defined (singular design, invalid statistic) it is shown as unavailable, not as 0. PVE from different models is not on a common basis and is not claimed to equal the value another program reports.
The figures are drawn with R (CMplot and base graphics). The Manhattan plot shows −log₁₀ p along the genome, one plot per model on its own scale, with the Bonferroni, suggestive and (when it was simulated) null-based lines; genome-wide hits are outlined and the names of the strongest ones, at most twelve, are written above the plot, with a strip of the marker density under the chromosomes. The QQ plot shows the p-value distribution of all models with λ, and the circos plot the genome-wide markers on a ring of chromosomes. Should R not be available, the program draws simpler built-in versions instead.

Trait Mapping · Chapter 18

Ranks candidate genes for a trait. It reads what public databases know about each gene — a trait annotation, its function, the pathways it is in, its orthologs in other species, and the papers that name it together with the trait — turns that into a score from 0 to 100. Give it the gene list of the QTL (the Gene_ID_list.txt written by Genes Extraction). It needs an internet connection, unlike the other tools.
Watch out. The score ranks genes by the evidence found in the databases. It is not the probability that a gene is causal, and a low score does not mean a gene is unimportant: many genes simply have little annotation. Where a database has nothing, the tool says so; it never fills a gap with an estimate.

Species — rice (Oryza sativa, IRGSP-1.0), wheat (Triticum aestivum) or maize (Zea mays). Chickpea is listed but cannot be used yet: it is not in Ensembl Plants or Gramene, so there is no verified source for its genes.

Trait — in words, for example Drought tolerance, Salt tolerance, Blast resistance, Grain yield. Related terms are added for you (drought: water deficit, osmotic stress, abscisic acid …); the terms used are listed on the Summary tab. Built-in vocabularies cover abiotic stress (drought, salt, heat, cold, submergence, oxidative, metal toxicity, alkalinity, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, micronutrients), biotic stress (fungal diseases: blast, brown spot, leaf spots and blotches, rusts, mildews, sheath blight, smuts and bunts, false smut, Fusarium / head blight / bakanae, aflatoxin and grain moulds, anthracnose, root and stem rots, wilts; bacterial diseases: bacterial blight and leaf streak, bacterial panicle blight; phytoplasmas; viruses; nematodes; insects and mites: planthoppers and leafhoppers, stem borers, armyworms and other caterpillars, aphids, thrips and other sap-sucking pests, gall midges and flies, storage pests, root pests; parasitic weeds such as Striga; weeds and herbicides; general disease resistance and defence), yield (grain size, grain number, tillering, harvest index, grain filling, heterosis), phenology and architecture (flowering, height, lodging, leaf angle, roots, seedling vigor, senescence, photosynthesis), seeds and reproduction (dormancy and pre-harvest sprouting, shattering, male sterility, apomixis) and quality (amylose / cooking quality, glycemic index and resistant starch, protein, oil, aroma, chalkiness, pigments and vitamins, anti-nutrients, sugar, fibre). A trait outside these groups is still searched by its own words, and the Summary tab says so; try the wording the databases use.
The genes to rank (below).

A gene ID list — paste IDs (one per line, or separated by commas, spaces or tabs) or choose a TXT / CSV / TSV / Excel file; the first column is read. For the genes of a QTL, use the Gene_ID_list.txt that Genes Extraction writes. Each gene receives up to five evidence scores between 0 and 1, which are combined with fixed weights:
 | Evidence | Weight | Where it comes from | What counts
 | Known gene–trait association | 30 % | Gramene (Trait Ontology annotation of the gene; QTL covering the gene counts less); Ensembl Plants phenotypes; for rice, the curated trait classes and Trait Ontology terms of Oryzabase | An annotation naming the trait or a related term. A direct trait term scores higher than a related one.
 | Functional relevance to the trait | 25 % | Gene description, GO terms and protein domains (Gramene, Ensembl Plants); for rice, the curated gene name of Oryzabase | Terms that match the trait words, weighted by the kind of GO evidence.
 | Pathway relevance | 20 % | Plant Reactome, Gramene | The gene is a member of a pathway whose name or summary matches the trait.
 | Ortholog evidence | 15 % | Ensembl Plants homology, Gramene gene tree | An ortholog (for example in Arabidopsis) that has a matching phenotype, description or trait term; one-to-one orthologs count more.
 | Literature support | 10 % | PubMed (NCBI E-utilities) | Papers in which the gene and the trait are named together. A title mention counts more than an abstract mention. This shows co-mention, not proof.
The final score is S = [Σ (weight × evidence) ÷ Σ weight] × 100, summed over the categories for which data could be retrieved. A category that is unavailable (for example the PubMed search failed) is left out and the other weights are scaled up — it is not treated as zero evidence. A category that was retrieved but found nothing relevant scores 0. Each piece of evidence is counted once, in one category only.

The evidence level summarises the final score: Direct association (a gene-level annotation names the trait or a close term), Multiple lines (three or more categories with evidence), Two lines, Single line, No trait evidence.

Several seconds per gene the first time (a run with about 150 candidate genes took about ten minutes in testing): every gene needs several requests to four services, which the tool spaces out to respect their limits. Start with a short list to try it out; the progress bar shows how far it is and Cancel stops it.

When a service is down. The run continues with the services that answer; a service that fails eight times in a row is skipped for the rest of the run, so the run never waits on it for hours. The evidence it could not get is shown as unavailable and listed in the Run information. If none can be reached the tool stops and says so; nothing is invented.
Gaps in the databases. Many plant genes have no description or GO annotation in Ensembl Plants / Gramene, and phenotype records are rare. Such a gene gets a low or empty score because the databases know little about it, not because it was judged unimportant.

section: Choosing K and the number of principal components
text:
Principal components used by K-means (default 0 = all). With all components K-means works in the full genotype space, so the PCA removes no noise. Population structure usually sits in the first few components: with a clear structure, 5 to 20 components give the same groups with less noise from the rest of the genome. The first components are always the ones kept, and the result states how many of the available components were used.
K-selection plot. Every run also draws the mean silhouette width (higher = better separated clusters) and the within-cluster sum of squares (the elbow) for K = 2 to 10, in the same space the clusters were found in. A red line marks the K you used and a gold line the K with the highest silhouette; the note under the plot names both. The plot is a guide, not a rule: choose K from what you know of the material (the number of parents, the breeding groups) and use the plot to check it. It can be downloaded as K selection (PNG).

The plot shows the samples on the first two principal components, coloured by cluster; the axis labels give the variance each component explains.
The K-selection plot below it (see above).

Decides which parents to cross. section: How the optimal plan is found
text:
For every cross among the candidates the tool calculates, with the R package SimpleMating (Lehermeier et al. 2017), the mean of the progeny from the marker effects, its standard deviation from the effects and the recombination along the map, and the usefulness = mean + selection intensity × standard deviation. A cross of two average parents that differ at many large-effect markers can have a higher usefulness than a cross of two good parents that are alike.
A plan is a list of crosses, each parent used in at most max crosses per parent of them. A parent in n of the N crosses contributes x = n / 2N to the next generation. A plan is scored by
Expected usefulness — the mean usefulness of the crosses of the plan.
Group coancestry — x′Cx, the relatedness of the next generation, from the relationship matrix calculated from the dosage matrix (VanRaden 2008; half of it is the coancestry); the lower, the more diversity is kept.
Progeny inbreeding — the mean coancestry between the two parents of each cross.
The penalty degree sets the balance: 0° maximises usefulness only, 90° minimises coancestry only. Usefulness and coancestry are rescaled to a common range and the plan with the highest cos(angle) × usefulness − sin(angle) × coancestry is searched by simulated annealing, which changes one parent of one cross at a time and keeps the plan valid (no selfing, no repeated cross, no parent over its limit). The search is repeated at 0°, 1°, 5°, 10° … 90° to draw the trade-off, and the longer search is made at your angle. The best angle is a choice: read the trade-off, then pick.

section: How the optimal plan is found
text: Note. The marker effects carry no intercept, so the values are on a relative scale: only the differences between crosses matter. Negate the effects for a trait where lower is better. Negative relationships are set to 0.

Optimal Plan: the crosses to make (with each cross's Usefulness, Cross Mean, Progeny SD and Kinship Coefficient), each parent's genomic value, number of crosses and contribution, and the usefulness / coancestry of the plan next to truncation selection (the best parents mated at random).
Usefulness versus diversity: the chart and table show the trade-off at every penalty degree.
Downloads: crossing plan, parent contributions, trade-off table (CSV) and the chart, the usefulness of all crosses, and the relationship matrix that was calculated.
Tip. A cross between two top parents is not always best: if they are close relatives the offspring lose diversity. Compare your plan with truncation selection and move the penalty degree until the usefulness you give up buys enough diversity.
Genomic Selection · Chapter 23

Trains a deep-learning model on a training population, predicts the genomic estimated breeding value (GEBV) of every possible hybrid between your parents, and screens them for
mid-parent (MPH) and better-parent (BPH) heterosis.

Three CSV files, plus one optional:
Training phenotype: column 0 = sample ID, column 1 = the numeric trait value (header row required).
 | Sample | Yield
 | Train001 | 3.252
 | Train002 | 3.995
 | Train003 | 8.577
 | Train004 | 2.6
Training genotype: first column = sample ID (the row label), then numeric marker columns.
 | Sample | SNP001 | SNP002 | SNP003 | SNP004 | SNP005 | SNP006 | …
 | Train001 | 0 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 0 | …
 | Train002 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 2 | 2 | …
 | Train003 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | …
 | Train004 | 0 | 2 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | …
Parent genotype: the candidate parents, with exactly the same marker columns as the training genotype.
 | Sample | SNP001 | SNP002 | SNP003 | SNP004 | SNP005 | SNP006 | …
 | Parent01 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 2 | …
 | Parent02 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | …
